decks.title: Citizenship, Part 1: Full and Equal Membership
goals: State the standard definition of citizenship and name its rights and obligations
Describe Marshall's civil, political and social rights
Explain how equal citizenship in practice needs attention to disadvantaged groups
Explain how nation-states set criteria and the general modes of acquiring citizenship in India

slides.heading: Citizenship: Full and Equal Membership

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: what citizenship is, three kinds of rights, struggles, equal rights in practice, and citizen and nation
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Who belongs to a political community, and on what terms? In this part we define citizenship, look at the rights and obligations it carries, see how people have struggled for equal citizenship, and ask what equality means in practice for different groups.

slides.heading: What citizenship means

rows: Standard definition
Full and equal membership of a political community, usually a nation-state
What it carries
Rights (civil, political and social) and obligations
Why it matters
It gives a person a recognised place and a claim to protection and a share in public life
Imagined case
A mason, Dinesh, who works in Kalvara is a full member of the country, not a guest

visual.alt: Table on citizenship: the standard definition is full and equal membership of a political community, usually a nation-state; it carries rights, civil, political and social, and obligations; it gives a recognised place, a claim to protection and a share in public life; an imagined mason Dinesh who works in Kalvara is a full member of the country
visual.caption: Kalvara and Dinesh are imagined.

slides.narration: Citizenship is full and equal membership of a political community, usually a nation state. It carries rights and obligations. visual.alt: Chart of the three kinds of citizenship rights described by T. H. Marshall. Civil rights protect individual freedom: speech, thought, faith, property and a fair hearing in court, for example an imagined worker Dinesh seeking his wages in a Kalvara court. Political rights are a share in power: voting and standing for office, for example an imagined resident Lata voting in a ward election. Social rights concern welfare and security: schooling and health care, for example a free school and clinic in every imagined ward. Citizenship also carries obligations: obey the laws, pay taxes and respect the rights of others
visual.caption: Marshall's three kinds of citizenship rights, with imagined examples.

slides.narration: This chart shows the scheme of T H Marshall, in his work Citizenship and Social Class of nineteen fifty. Civil rights protect individual freedom. Political rights give a share in power, such as voting. Social rights concern welfare and security, such as schooling and health care. Citizenship also carries obligations, such as obeying the laws and paying taxes.

slides.heading: Obligations of citizens

rows: Obey the laws
Follow the rules that the community has made
A shopkeeper keeps to the market rules
Pay taxes
Contribute to the cost of public services
A trader pays the tax due on her sales
Respect the rights of others
Do not harm the equal rights of fellow citizens
A landlord does not refuse tenants on grounds of caste

visual.alt: Table of obligations of citizens: obey the laws, pay taxes and respect the rights of others, each with an imagined case in Kalvara
visual.caption: The cases in Kalvara are imagined.

slides.narration: Rights come with obligations. A citizen should obey the laws, pay taxes, and respect the rights of others. These obligations matter because the community can protect everyone only if its members also do their part. An imagined shopkeeper in Kalvara keeps to the market rules, and a landlord does not refuse tenants on grounds of caste.

slides.heading: Struggles for equal citizenship

rows: French Revolution, 1789
That people be citizens with equal rights and not subjects ranked by birth
Struggle against apartheid in South Africa
Equal citizenship for all people; apartheid ended in the early 1990s and the first democratic election was in 1994
Women's movements in India
Equal rights and a full place as citizens
Movements of Dalits in India
An end to untouchability and equal treatment and dignity as citizens

visual.alt: Table of struggles for equal citizenship: the French Revolution of 1789 demanded equal rights for citizens; the struggle against apartheid in South Africa demanded equal citizenship, apartheid ended in the early 1990s and the first democratic election was in 1994; women's movements in India demanded equal rights; movements of Dalits in India demanded an end to untouchability and equal dignity

slides.narration: Equal citizenship was won through struggle. The French Revolution of seventeen eighty nine stressed that people are citizens with equal rights, not subjects ranked by birth. In South Africa the struggle against apartheid ended it in the early nineteen nineties, and the first democratic election was in nineteen ninety four. In India, movements of women and of Dalits demanded equal rights and dignity.

slides.narration: This web shows four areas where equal citizenship is tested in practice. Citizens may move and work anywhere. The urban poor ask for housing and services. Forest dwellers depend on the forest for their livelihood. Women and Dalits struggled for equal treatment. The common thread is that the same rule for all may fall unequally, so disadvantaged groups need attention.

slides.heading: Freedom to move and work

rows: The freedom
A citizen may move freely and live and work in any part of the country (Article 19), subject to reasonable restrictions
Why it fits equal citizenship
India has a single citizenship, so a citizen of any state is a full member everywhere
One view on arrivals
Some argue that arrivals strain housing, jobs and services
Another view
Others argue that they are equal citizens who add to the economy; claims should be tested with evidence
Imagined case
Dinesh, from a distant state, seeks a room in Kalvara

slides.heading: Citizen and nation

rows: Who decides
Each nation-state sets criteria for citizenship by its own law
India
Part II of the Constitution and the Citizenship Act 1955 provide for citizenship, as provided in the Act, which has been amended over time
General modes
Birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory
Single citizenship
There is one citizenship for the whole country and none separate for each state
The principle
As the Constitution intends, citizenship is equal for all, without distinction of religion, caste or gender

sections.heading: 1. What citizenship means
sections.body_md: **Citizenship** is full and **equal membership** of a political community, usually a nation-state. It carries **rights** and **obligations**. Obligations include obeying the laws, paying taxes and respecting the rights of others.

key_terms.definition_md: Full and equal membership of a political community, usually a nation-state.
A political community organised as a state, whose members are its citizens.
A duty that a citizen owes to the community, such as obeying the laws and paying taxes.

sections.heading: 2. Marshall's three kinds of rights
sections.body_md:
**T. H. Marshall** (*Citizenship and Social Class*, 1950) divided citizenship rights into three kinds.

- **Civil rights**: individual freedom, such as speech, thought, faith, property and a fair hearing in court.
- **Political rights**: a share in power, such as voting and standing for office.
- **Social rights**: welfare and security, such as schooling and health care.

key_terms.definition_md: Rights that protect individual freedom, such as speech, property and a fair hearing in court.
Rights that give a share in power, such as voting and standing for office.

sections.heading: 3. Struggles for equal citizenship
sections.body_md: Equal citizenship was won through **struggle**. The **French Revolution** (1789) stressed that people are citizens with equal rights. The struggle against **apartheid** in South Africa, a system of racial discrimination, ended it in the early 1990s, and the first democratic election was held in **1994**. In India, **women's movements** and movements of **Dalits** demanded equal rights, an end to untouchability and dignity.

key_terms.definition_md: A system of racial discrimination in South Africa that denied equal citizenship to most people; it ended in the early 1990s.
The principle that every citizen is a full member of the political community, whatever his or her group.

rows: French Revolution, 1789

Struggle against apartheid in South Africa
Equal citizenship for all people; apartheid ended in the early 1990s and the first democratic election was in 1994
Women's movements in India
Equal rights and a full place as citizens
Movements of Dalits in India
An end to untouchability and equal treatment and dignity as citizens

sections.heading: 4. Equal rights in practice
sections.body_md:
A citizen may **move freely and live and work** in any part of the country (Article 19), subject to reasonable restrictions. Some argue that arrivals strain housing, jobs and services, and others that they are equal citizens who add to the economy; claims should be tested with evidence.

The **urban poor** have a fair claim to housing, water and schools, weighed with the city plan. **Tribal people and forest dwellers** depend on the forest for livelihood, which must be weighed with protecting it.

The common thread: the same rule for all may fall unequally, so equal citizenship needs **attention to disadvantaged groups**.

key_terms.definition_md: One citizenship for the whole country, with none separate for each state, as in India.
A group whose circumstances make it harder to use its rights equally with others.

sections.heading: 5. Citizen and nation
sections.body_md:
Each **nation-state** sets criteria for citizenship by its own law. In India, **Part II** of the Constitution and the **Citizenship Act 1955** provide for citizenship, as provided in the Act, which has been amended over time. The general modes are **birth**, **descent**, **registration**, **naturalisation** and **incorporation of territory**.

As the Constitution intends, India gives citizenship **equally to all**, without distinction of religion, caste or gender.

key_terms.definition_md: Citizenship that passes to a person born abroad through a parent who is a citizen.
The grant of citizenship to a foreigner who meets the conditions laid down in law.
Acquisition of citizenship by the residents of territory that is added to a state.

sections.heading: 6. Universal citizenship
sections.body_md:
The ideal of **universal citizenship** is that every person should be a citizen of some state, with full rights. The **Universal Declaration of Human Rights** (1948) says that everyone has the right to a nationality.

A **refugee** is forced to leave a country by persecution, war or violence. A **stateless person** is considered a citizen by no state. **UNHCR**, the United Nations refugee agency (created 1950), works to protect refugees.

States face difficult choices. Some argue that a state has a **humanitarian duty** to shelter people in danger; others stress **limits** on housing and services and the need for **security checks**.

sections.heading: 7. Global citizenship
sections.body_md:
**Global citizenship** is the idea that we belong to a **world community** and have responsibilities toward humanity: the environment, human rights and disaster relief. It is easier to practise because of the **internet** and communication.

Some argue that it can **complement** national citizenship. Others argue that **national citizenship** remains the main source of rights and protection, since states enforce rights. Students present both views with reasons and then judge.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying citizenship means only the right to vote: name civil, political and social rights and the obligations.
- Mixing up the three kinds of rights: civil protects freedom, political gives a share in power, social gives welfare.
- Taking a side on arrivals from other states: give both views with reasons and keep every citizen's right in view.
- Listing the modes without saying they are as provided in the Act, amended over time.
- Using refugee and stateless as the same word: define each.
- Saying global citizenship means a world state: it is an idea of belonging and responsibility.
- Leaving out the internet, or backing one side in the debate on how global and national citizenship relate.

**Tips:** begin with the standard definition; give a short imagined example; present both views, then judge with reasons.

questions.stem_md: In political theory, citizenship is best defined as

options.text_md: living in one city for a number of years
full and equal membership of a political community, usually a nation-state
owning land inside a country
a licence to vote granted by a ruler

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** full and equal membership of a political community, usually a nation-state. Citizenship is full and equal membership of a political community, usually a nation-state, and it carries rights and obligations. Length of residence, land ownership and a ruler's licence do not define it.

questions.stem_md: The division of citizenship rights into civil, political and social rights is linked with

options.text_md: John Rawls, in A Theory of Justice (1971)
Immanuel Kant, on human dignity
Isaiah Berlin, on two kinds of liberty
T. H. Marshall, in Citizenship and Social Class (1950)

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** T. H. Marshall, in Citizenship and Social Class (1950). T. H. Marshall wrote Citizenship and Social Class in 1950 and set out the three kinds of rights. Rawls is linked with the veil of ignorance, Kant with dignity and Berlin with negative and positive liberty.

questions.stem_md: Which list names the three kinds of citizenship rights in Marshall's scheme?

options.text_md: Civil, political and social rights
Civil, criminal and commercial rights
Economic, military and religious rights
Local, state and national rights

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Civil, political and social rights. Marshall spoke of civil, political and social rights. The other lists mix up the names of laws, areas of activity or levels of government and are not his scheme.

questions.stem_md: Dinesh, a worker who has come to the imagined city of Kalvara from a distant state, speaks freely at a workers' meeting and approaches a court when his contractor refuses his wages. These freedoms are mainly

options.text_md: political rights
social rights
civil rights
obligations of a citizen

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** civil rights. Freedom of speech and access to a fair hearing are civil rights, which protect the individual's freedom. Political rights concern voting and holding office, social rights concern welfare and security, and obligations are duties and not freedoms.

questions.stem_md: Lata, aged nineteen, has her name entered in the voters' list of imagined Kalvara and later stands for a ward committee. Which kind of citizenship rights is she using?

options.text_md: Civil rights
Social rights
Political rights
None, since rights need a licence

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Political rights. Voting and standing for office are the political rights, which let a citizen take part in the exercise of power. Civil rights protect individual freedoms and social rights concern welfare, and rights do not depend on a licence.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Kalvara Corporation runs free primary schools and a basic clinic in every ward so that every family can have schooling and a minimum of health care. Which kind of citizenship rights does this mainly serve?

options.text_md: Social rights
Political rights
Civil rights
Obligations

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Social rights. Schooling and health care serve the social rights, which concern economic welfare and security. Voting is political, freedom of speech and a fair trial are civil, and obligations are the duties of citizens.

questions.stem_md: Citizenship carries obligations as well as rights. Which pair is a correct example of obligations?

options.text_md: Voting and standing for office
Speaking freely and owning property
Getting schooling and health care
Obeying the laws and paying taxes

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Obeying the laws and paying taxes. Obeying the laws and paying taxes are obligations that a citizen owes to the community. The other pairs are examples of political, civil and social rights.

questions.stem_md: The French Revolution of 1789 is linked with the history of equal citizenship because it

options.text_md: created one government for the whole world
declared that people were citizens with equal rights and not subjects ranked by birth
ended apartheid in South Africa
gave every adult in India a vote

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** declared that people were citizens with equal rights and not subjects ranked by birth. The Revolution put forward the idea that people are citizens with equal rights, against privileges of birth. It did not create a world government, and apartheid and the Indian vote belong to other histories.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about the struggle against apartheid in South Africa is correct?

options.text_md: Apartheid ended in the early 1990s and the first democratic election took place in 1994
Apartheid ended in the 1960s and the first democratic election took place in 1970
Apartheid continues as law in South Africa today
The first democratic election took place in 1789

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Apartheid ended in the early 1990s and the first democratic election took place in 1994. Apartheid, a system of racial discrimination that denied equal citizenship to most people, ended in the early 1990s, and the first democratic election was held in 1994. The other dates and claims are wrong.

questions.stem_md: Dinesh is a citizen of India from a distant state who wishes to live and work in imagined Kalvara. Which principle supports his claim?

options.text_md: Only natives of a city may work in it
A citizen may move freely and live and work in any part of the country, subject to reasonable restrictions
A worker must remain in the state of his birth
Freedom of movement belongs only to the residents of large cities

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A citizen may move freely and live and work in any part of the country, subject to reasonable restrictions. Article 19 gives citizens the freedom to move freely and to reside and work in any part of the territory, subject to reasonable restrictions. A birthplace test and a city-size test have no basis in that freedom.

questions.stem_md: At an imagined meeting in Kalvara, one resident says that workers from other states strain housing and jobs, while another says they are citizens with an equal right to work who also add to the city's economy. Which response is the most balanced?

options.text_md: Accept the first claim and ignore the second
Say that workers from other states are not citizens
Examine both claims with evidence while remembering that every citizen has the right to move and work
Accept the second claim and deny that housing or jobs can ever be strained

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Examine both claims with evidence while remembering that every citizen has the right to move and work. A balanced reply tests both claims with evidence and keeps in view the equal right of every citizen. Ignoring one claim, or denying the citizenship of the workers, is not balanced.

questions.stem_md: Residents of the imagined Harbour Lane settlement in Kalvara petition for piped water and a nearby school, saying that they are citizens like any others. Their petition mainly rests on the idea that

options.text_md: only owners of registered houses are citizens
basic services are a favour that may be refused at will
citizenship ends at the boundary of a city
equal citizenship includes a fair claim to basic services wherever a citizen lives

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** equal citizenship includes a fair claim to basic services wherever a citizen lives. The petitioners argue that they are full and equal members and so have a fair claim to basic services. Citizenship does not depend on owning a registered house, and services are not merely a favour.

questions.stem_md: For generations the imagined villagers of the Sarna Hills have gathered fruit and fuelwood in the Dhanvi Forest. A new notice bans all entry in order to protect rare trees. Which statement best fits equal citizenship?

options.text_md: Forest dwellers are not citizens and need not be heard
Only the protection of the forest matters
Only the livelihood claim matters and protection may be dropped
The villagers' livelihood and the aim of protecting the forest both deserve weighing, so that a disadvantaged group is not overlooked

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The villagers' livelihood and the aim of protecting the forest both deserve weighing, so that a disadvantaged group is not overlooked. Equal citizenship asks that a vulnerable group be heard, while protecting the forest is also a legitimate aim, so both are weighed with reasons. Excluding the villagers or dropping either aim does not do this.

questions.stem_md: A rule in imagined Kalvara says that every family must collect its ration card in person from the Corporation office on a weekday morning. Many daily-wage workers lose a day's earnings if they go. What does this show about equal citizenship?

options.text_md: Equal rules always bring equal results
Daily-wage workers are not citizens
One rule for all can still leave some people at a disadvantage, so equal citizenship needs attention to their circumstances
Rules for citizens should never be written

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** One rule for all can still leave some people at a disadvantage, so equal citizenship needs attention to their circumstances. The same rule falls more heavily on those who lose a day's earnings, so equal citizenship needs attention to disadvantaged groups. Equal rules do not always bring equal results, and the workers are citizens.

questions.stem_md: The imagined country of Torvania gives citizenship to a child born abroad if at least one parent is a Torvanian citizen. This mode of acquiring citizenship is called

options.text_md: citizenship by naturalisation
citizenship by descent
citizenship by incorporation of territory
citizenship by birth within its territory

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** citizenship by descent. Citizenship that passes through a citizen parent to a child born abroad is citizenship by descent. Naturalisation applies to a foreigner who meets conditions, incorporation to residents of added territory, and birth to a person born within the country.

questions.stem_md: By a treaty the imagined country of Torvania takes in the neighbouring region of Brennick, and the residents of Brennick become Torvanian citizens under the treaty law. This is citizenship by

options.text_md: incorporation of territory
descent
birth to citizen parents
naturalisation after long residence

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** incorporation of territory. When territory is added to a state and its residents become citizens by law, citizenship comes by incorporation of territory. Descent and birth depend on parentage or place of birth, and naturalisation on an individual's application.

questions.stem_md: In India, citizenship is provided for in

options.text_md: Part III of the Constitution alone, with no Act
Part II of the Constitution and the Citizenship Act 1955, as amended over time
separate laws made by each state for its own citizens
a rule issued by the Election Commission

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Part II of the Constitution and the Citizenship Act 1955, as amended over time. Part II of the Constitution and the Citizenship Act 1955, amended over time, deal with citizenship. Part III is on fundamental rights, there is one citizenship for the country and not one for each state, and the Election Commission does not make citizenship rules.

questions.stem_md: A pamphlet circulated in imagined Kalvara claims that members of one caste hold a lesser kind of citizenship than others. Which constitutional principle contradicts this claim?

options.text_md: Citizenship is graded by caste in each state
Citizenship is a privilege of wealthy families
Citizenship depends on the language one speaks
India gives citizenship equally to all, without distinction of religion, caste or gender

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** India gives citizenship equally to all, without distinction of religion, caste or gender. The Constitution intends that citizenship be equal for all, without distinction of religion, caste or gender. Grading by caste, wealth or language has no place in it.

questions.stem_md: A refugee is best described as a person who

options.text_md: has been forced to leave his or her country by persecution, war or violence and cannot safely return
moves to another city for better pay
travels abroad for a holiday
holds the citizenship of two countries

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** has been forced to leave his or her country by persecution, war or violence and cannot safely return. A refugee flees danger such as persecution, war or violence and cannot safely go back. A person moving for pay or a holiday traveller is not a refugee, and holding two citizenships is dual citizenship.

questions.stem_md: A stateless person is one who

options.text_md: lives in a village far from the capital
has lost his or her job
is not considered a citizen by any state
holds passports of two states

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** is not considered a citizen by any state. A stateless person is not treated as a citizen by any state. Distance from a capital, loss of a job and holding two passports do not make a person stateless.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Marlen family was born in the country of Ostrell, but Ostrell's law does not recognise them and no other state does either. They cannot obtain school admission, a bank account or a travel document. This best illustrates

options.text_md: the benefits of dual citizenship
citizenship by naturalisation
the problem of statelessness: without citizenship a person may lack the rights and protection that membership gives
an example of global citizenship

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** the problem of statelessness: without citizenship a person may lack the rights and protection that membership gives. A family that no state recognises is stateless and lacks the rights and protection that citizenship gives. Dual citizenship and naturalisation are ways of having citizenship, and global citizenship is a different idea about belonging to a world community.

questions.stem_md: The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) is

options.text_md: the United Nations agency that works to protect refugees
a court that decides citizenship disputes of every country
the legislature of the United Nations
a trade organisation of states

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the United Nations agency that works to protect refugees. UNHCR is the United Nations refugee agency and works to protect refugees. It is not a world court, a legislature or a trade body.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about nationality is found in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 1948?

options.text_md: Only citizens of large states have the right to a nationality
A state may take away nationality arbitrarily
Nationality belongs only to those born in a capital city
Everyone has the right to a nationality

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Everyone has the right to a nationality. The Declaration says that everyone has a right to a nationality, which supports the ideal of universal citizenship. The other statements contradict it.

questions.stem_md: The imagined state of Torvania debates whether to admit people fleeing a conflict across its border. One minister stresses a duty to give shelter to people in danger, while another points to limits on housing and public services and the need for security checks. Which reading is the most balanced?

options.text_md: Only the first minister speaks of values, so the second may be ignored
Each minister names a real consideration, so the state must weigh humanitarian duty against practical limits and give its reasons
Only the second minister is practical, so the first may be ignored
A state has no choices to make in such a matter

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Each minister names a real consideration, so the state must weigh humanitarian duty against practical limits and give its reasons. A balanced reading sees humanitarian duty and practical limits as both real and asks the state to weigh them with reasons. Ignoring either minister, or saying that no choice exists, is not balanced.

questions.stem_md: Global citizenship is the idea that

options.text_md: people belong to a world community and have responsibilities toward humanity as a whole
a world government issues a passport to every person
national citizenship should be abolished
only wealthy people may travel across borders

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** people belong to a world community and have responsibilities toward humanity as a whole. Global citizenship is the idea of belonging to a world community with responsibilities toward humanity. It does not mean a world state, the end of national citizenship or any rule about travel.

questions.stem_md: How does the internet help the idea of global citizenship?

options.text_md: It replaces the laws of every country
It lets people in different countries learn about, discuss and act on shared concerns with ease
It gives every user citizenship of all states
It prevents disasters from happening

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** It lets people in different countries learn about, discuss and act on shared concerns with ease. The internet makes communication across borders easy, so people can learn about and act on shared concerns. It does not replace laws, grant citizenship or prevent disasters.

questions.stem_md: At the imagined Lumen Global Youth Forum, students from many countries run an online drive to plant trees and to raise money for flood relief in a country none of them lives in. Which responsibilities of global citizenship do they show?

options.text_md: Compulsory service in a national army
Payment of taxes to a world government
Care for the environment and help in disasters
Voting in the elections of a foreign state

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Care for the environment and help in disasters. Planting trees and relief for flood victims show care for the environment and help in disasters, which are responsibilities of global citizenship. There is no world government, army service or foreign voting involved.

questions.stem_md: At the imagined Lumen Forum, Pedro says that global citizenship should replace national citizenship, while Mei says that national citizenship stays the main source of rights. Which statement best evaluates the debate?

options.text_md: Pedro is right, because states no longer exist
Mei is right, because global concerns are not real
The matter has been settled by law for all countries
Some hold that global citizenship can complement national citizenship, while others hold that rights are secured mainly through states, and each view needs reasons

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Some hold that global citizenship can complement national citizenship, while others hold that rights are secured mainly through states, and each view needs reasons. The debate has several positions: some see global citizenship as a complement to national citizenship, others see states as the main source of rights. States still exist, global concerns are real, and no law settles the debate.

questions.stem_md: Why do some argue that national citizenship remains the main source of rights and protection?

options.text_md: Because people should care only about their own countrymen
Because nations are older than humanity
Because the United Nations can punish any person
Because states have the laws, courts and officials that enforce rights within their territory

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Because states have the laws, courts and officials that enforce rights within their territory. Those who hold this view point out that states have the laws, courts and officials that enforce rights. It does not follow that people should care for no one else, and the United Nations has no power to punish individuals everywhere.

options.text_md: True

They agree on a form of help, such as a fund or a tree-planting drive

questions.stem_md: What is meant by citizenship? Name one kind of right that it carries.
questions.solution_md: Definition and a right.

answer.model_answer_md: **Citizenship** means being a full and **equal member** of a political community, most often a nation-state. A citizen holds rights, for example **civil**, **political** or **social** rights, and also owes obligations.

marking_scheme.step: Full and equal membership of a political community, usually a nation-state

questions.stem_md: Who divided citizenship rights into three kinds, and what are they?
questions.solution_md: Name and three kinds.

answer.model_answer_md: **T. H. Marshall**, in *Citizenship and Social Class* (1950), divided them into **civil rights** (individual freedoms), **political rights** (a share in power, such as voting) and **social rights** (welfare and security).

questions.stem_md: Citizenship carries obligations as well as rights. Give two obligations of a citizen and say why they matter.
questions.solution_md: Two obligations and a reason.

answer.model_answer_md: A citizen should **obey the laws** and **pay taxes**, and should respect the rights of others. They matter because the community can protect everyone's **rights** only if its members also do their part.

marking_scheme.step: A reason: rights are sustained by the duties of members

questions.stem_md: How does the struggle against apartheid in South Africa illustrate the demand for equal citizenship?
questions.solution_md: Denial of equality, the struggle, and dates.

answer.model_answer_md: Under **apartheid**, most people were denied equal rights by a system of racial discrimination. Their struggle demanded **full and equal citizenship**. Apartheid ended in the early 1990s, and the first **democratic election** was held in 1994.

marking_scheme.step: Apartheid denied equal rights through racial discrimination, and the struggle demanded equal citizenship
Ended in the early 1990s; first democratic election in 1994

questions.stem_md: A citizen from a distant state is refused a rented room in imagined Kalvara only because he is from another state. Which right is involved and what does equal citizenship say?
questions.solution_md: Right and principle.

answer.model_answer_md: The case concerns the citizen's **freedom to move and to live and work** in any part of the country. Equal citizenship means that he is a **full member** of the country and not a stranger, though **reasonable restrictions** may apply.

marking_scheme.step: Freedom to move, live and work anywhere in the country
Equal, single citizenship; reasonable restrictions only

questions.stem_md: Residents of the imagined Harbour Lane settlement ask for water and drainage. Explain how equal citizenship supports their claim, and name one view that others may hold.
questions.solution_md: Claim and a different view.

answer.model_answer_md: As **citizens**, they are full and equal members and so have a fair claim to **basic services** and housing. Others may argue that the land is subject to **planning rules**, so the Corporation must weigh the claim against such rules.

marking_scheme.step: Citizens have a fair claim to basic services whatever their place of residence
Another view: planning or land rules must be weighed

questions.stem_md: Why should the livelihood of forest dwellers, such as the imagined villagers of the Sarna Hills, be considered in a debate on equal citizenship?
questions.solution_md: Citizenship and livelihood.

answer.model_answer_md: Forest dwellers are **full citizens** whose **livelihood** depends on gathering produce from the forest. Equal citizenship asks that such a disadvantaged group be **heard** and that the aim of protecting the forest be weighed with it.

marking_scheme.step: They are full citizens whose livelihood depends on the forest
A disadvantaged group must be heard and the claims weighed

questions.stem_md: What is a stateless person? Give one difficulty that the imagined Marlen family might face.
questions.solution_md: Meaning and a difficulty.

answer.model_answer_md: A **stateless person** is one whom no state treats as a citizen. The Marlen family may be unable to get **school admission** or a travel document, because they lack the **rights and protection** that citizenship gives.

marking_scheme.step: Not considered a citizen by any state
A difficulty such as lack of rights, schooling or travel documents

questions.stem_md: What is a refugee, and what does the United Nations refugee agency do?
questions.solution_md: Refugee and agency.

answer.model_answer_md: A **refugee** is a person forced to leave his or her country by persecution, war or violence and unable to return safely. The **United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees**, UNHCR, works to **protect** refugees.

marking_scheme.step: A person forced to flee persecution, war or violence and unable to return safely

questions.stem_md: What is global citizenship, and how has the internet made it easier to practise?
questions.solution_md: Idea and the role of communication.

answer.model_answer_md: **Global citizenship** is the idea that we belong to a **world community** with responsibilities toward humanity. The **internet** and modern communication help people in different countries to learn about shared concerns and act together.

marking_scheme.step: Belonging to a world community with responsibilities toward humanity
The internet and communication make contact and joint action easy

questions.stem_md: Name the general modes by which citizenship may be acquired in India, giving an imagined example of one.
questions.solution_md: Modes named, with the Act and an example.

answer.model_answer_md: As provided in the Citizenship Act 1955, which has been **amended over time**, citizenship may be acquired by **birth**, **descent**, **registration**, **naturalisation** and **incorporation of territory**. For example, a child born abroad to a citizen parent may be a citizen **by descent**, as in imagined Torvania.

marking_scheme.step: The Citizenship Act 1955, amended over time
Birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory
A suitable example of one mode

questions.stem_md: Explain the constitutional principle of equal citizenship in India, and how it differs from a system of separate state citizenships.
questions.solution_md: Equality, single citizenship, effect.

answer.model_answer_md: The Constitution intends that citizenship be given **equally to all**, without distinction of **religion, caste or gender**. India also has a **single citizenship** for the whole country, so a citizen from any state is a **full member** everywhere and may in general live and work in any part.

marking_scheme.step: Citizenship equal for all without distinction of religion, caste or gender
A single citizenship for the whole country
Effect: a citizen is a full member in every state

questions.stem_md: Explain why equal citizenship requires attention to disadvantaged groups, using the imagined ration card rule in Kalvara or any other example.
questions.solution_md: Same rule, unequal effect, attention needed.

answer.model_answer_md: A rule that is **the same for all** may still fall unequally. If every family must collect its ration card in person on a weekday, **daily-wage workers** lose earnings. So equal citizenship requires attention to such **disadvantaged groups**, for example through other ways of applying, so that all can use their **rights** equally.

marking_scheme.step: The same rule for all can have unequal effects
Attention to disadvantaged groups so that all can use their rights equally

questions.stem_md: Present, without taking a side, the two views at an imagined meeting in Kalvara on workers who have come from other states.
questions.solution_md: Both views, then evidence.

answer.model_answer_md: Some residents argue that arrivals strain **housing, jobs and services**. Others argue that the workers are **citizens** with an equal right to **move and work**, and that they add to the city's economy. Both claims should be examined with **evidence**, keeping in mind that every citizen has this right.

marking_scheme.step: One view: strain on housing, jobs and services
Other view: equal right to move and work, contribution to the economy
Both examined with evidence, the right of every citizen kept in view

questions.stem_md: Describe the difficult choices that a state such as imagined Torvania faces when people fleeing a conflict ask to be admitted. Present both views.
questions.solution_md: Duty, limits and weighing.

answer.model_answer_md: One view holds that a state owes shelter to people in danger, as a **humanitarian duty**. Another view points to **limits** of housing and public services and to the need for **security checks**. The state must **weigh** these and give its reasons, and citizens may judge with reasons.

marking_scheme.step: The state weighs them and gives reasons

questions.stem_md: Give the views of those who say global citizenship can complement national citizenship and of those who say national citizenship remains the main source of rights.
questions.solution_md: Both views with reasons.

answer.model_answer_md: Some argue that people can be loyal to their nation and also care for **humanity**, for example in the **environment** or **disaster relief**, so global citizenship **complements** national citizenship. Others argue that **states** have the laws and courts that enforce rights, so national citizenship remains the **main source** of rights.

marking_scheme.step: National citizenship the main source, with the reason that states enforce rights

questions.stem_md: The imagined Dhanvi Forest is closed to all entry to protect rare trees, though the villagers of the Sarna Hills depend on it. Show how equal citizenship and the aim of protection may both be considered.
questions.solution_md: Both claims weighed.

answer.model_answer_md: The villagers are **full citizens** whose **livelihood** depends on the forest, and equal citizenship requires that their claim be heard. Protecting rare trees is also a **legitimate aim**. The authorities may **weigh** both, hold consultations, and seek arrangements, such as regulated gathering, that give **reasons** to each side.

marking_scheme.step: Villagers are full citizens whose livelihood must be heard
Protection is also a legitimate aim
Weighing the two, with consultation and reasons

questions.stem_md: Explain the idea of citizenship, with its rights and obligations, using the three kinds of rights described by T. H. Marshall.
questions.solution_md: Definition, Marshall, three kinds, obligations.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Citizenship** means being a full and **equal member** of a political community, most often a nation-state.
2. **T. H. Marshall** (*Citizenship and Social Class*, 1950) divided the rights into three kinds.
3. **Civil rights** protect individual freedoms, such as speech and a fair hearing; **political rights** are a share in power, such as voting.
4. **Social rights** cover welfare and the safety net of each citizen, for example access to schools and clinics.
5. Citizens also have **obligations**, such as obeying the laws and paying taxes.

marking_scheme.step: Marshall and his three kinds named

questions.stem_md: Describe struggles in history and in India for equal citizenship.
questions.solution_md: Four struggles, with dates.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **French Revolution** of 1789 stressed that people are citizens with equal rights, not subjects ranked by birth.
2. In **South Africa**, the struggle against apartheid, which denied equality by racial discrimination, led to its end in the early 1990s.
3. The first **democratic election** there was held in 1994.
4. In India, **women's movements** demanded equal rights.
5. Movements of **Dalits** sought equal treatment and dignity as full citizens.

marking_scheme.step: End in the early 1990s; election in 1994

questions.stem_md: Using imagined cases from Kalvara, the Harbour Lane settlement and the Sarna Hills, explain how equal citizenship in practice requires attention to disadvantaged groups.
questions.solution_md: Movement, services, urban poor, forest dwellers, disadvantage.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Equal citizens may **move and work** anywhere, so a worker from another state in Kalvara is a full member, subject to reasonable restrictions.
2. People may differ on **pressure on services**, so claims should be tested with evidence.
3. The **urban poor** of Harbour Lane ask for housing, water and services as citizens.
4. **Forest dwellers** of the Sarna Hills depend on the forest, and their livelihood must be weighed with protection.
5. **Same rules** can fall unequally, so disadvantaged groups need attention.

marking_scheme.step: Freedom to move and work, with reasonable restrictions
Neutral treatment of the debate on migrants
Forest dwellers, livelihood weighed with protection
Same rules can fall unequally, so attention to disadvantaged groups

questions.stem_md: Explain how nation-states set criteria for citizenship, with reference to the general modes of acquiring citizenship in India and the constitutional principle of equal citizenship.
questions.solution_md: Criteria, Part II and Act, modes, single citizenship, equality.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. A **nation-state** decides by law who is a citizen, so criteria differ.
2. In India, **Part II** of the Constitution and the **Citizenship Act 1955**, amended over time, provide for citizenship.
3. The Act provides for **birth**, **descent**, **registration**, **naturalisation** and **incorporation of territory**.
4. India has a **single citizenship** for the whole country.
5. As the Constitution intends, it is given **equally**, without distinction of religion, caste or gender.

marking_scheme.step: Part II and the Citizenship Act 1955, amended over time
Equality without distinction of religion, caste or gender

questions.stem_md: Explain the ideal of universal citizenship and the problems of refugees and stateless persons, and present the different views on the choices that states face.
questions.solution_md: Ideal, refugees, stateless persons, UNHCR, views.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **ideal** is that every person should be a citizen somewhere, with full rights.
2. A **refugee** has been forced to leave a country by persecution, war or violence.
3. A **stateless person** is considered a citizen by no state and may lack rights and protection.
4. The **United Nations refugee agency**, UNHCR, works to protect refugees.
5. Some argue that states have a **duty** to shelter people in danger, while others stress practical **limits**, and states must weigh them.

marking_scheme.step: Stateless person defined and the difficulties
Both views of states presented with reasons

questions.stem_md: Explain the idea of global citizenship and the role of the internet, and discuss the views on whether it can complement national citizenship.
questions.solution_md: Idea, responsibilities, internet, both views.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Global citizenship** is the idea that we belong to a **world community** with responsibilities toward humanity.
2. These include care for the **environment**, **human rights** and **disaster relief**.
3. The **internet** and communication make shared action across borders easier.
4. Some argue that it can **complement** national citizenship.
5. Others argue that **national citizenship** remains the main source of rights and protection, since states enforce rights; the student judges with reasons.

marking_scheme.step: National citizenship the main source, with a reasoned judgement

questions.stem_md: Read the petition and answer the questions that follow. *(An imagined petition written by SOYL for practice; Kalvara, the Harbour Lane settlement and its residents are not real.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Water and schooling concern welfare and security.

**(b)** Voting and paying taxes.

**(c) (i)** Two reasonable points.

**OR (c) (ii)** A fair response.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Social rights**.

**(b)** The right to **vote** (a political right) and the obligation to **pay taxes**.

**(c) (i)** The residents point to their **equal citizenship** and their need for basic services. The planning member points to **land reserved** under the city plan and to limited funds. Both are reasonable, so a **hearing** can weigh them.

**OR (c) (ii)** The Corporation might hold a **hearing**, provide water through **common taps** at once and plan longer-term services. This respects the families' **equal claim** as citizens while the plan and funds are also considered.

questions.passage_md:
**From a petition of the residents of Harbour Lane to the Kalvara Corporation, imagined**

We are four hundred families who have lived at Harbour Lane for many years. We vote in the ward election and pay the taxes on what we buy, yet we have no piped water, and our children walk far to a school. We are citizens like everyone in the city. A member of the planning committee replied that part of our land is reserved under the city plan, and that the Corporation has limited funds. We ask for a hearing so that both our needs and the plan can be weighed.

children.stem_md: Which kind of citizenship rights is the petition mainly asking for when it asks for water and schooling?
children.solution_md: Water and schooling concern welfare and security.

answer.model_answer_md: **Social rights**.

children.stem_md: Name one right and one obligation of citizenship that the residents say they already use or meet.
